attestations.source_text: Sometimes you need to be very specific when identifying things. To do so, you use demonstrative adjectives (this, that, these, those).
Possessive adjectives modify nouns and are used to express relationship and ownership. They agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
Possessive pronouns replace nouns used with possessive adjectives. They agree in gender and number with the noun they replace, not with the possessor.
Remember that the most common way of expressing possession is by using être à + the disjunctive pronoun.

attestations.source_text: The possessive pronoun is also often used with aussi and non plus to confirm an affirmative or negative statement.
A demonstrative pronoun replaces a demonstrative adjective + a noun. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it replaces.
Compound demonstrative pronouns are used to compare elements of the same nature or to indicate a choice between two objects or two people.
The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and is often the subject of the verb être. It refers to an idea previously introduced.
The indefinite demonstrative pronouns ceci (this), cela (that), and ça (this/that, familiar) refer to indefinite things or ideas.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Demonstrative adjectives agree in gender and number
grammar_rules.summary: Demonstrative adjectives (ce, cet, cette, ces) agree with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.explanation: Demonstrative adjectives point out specific nouns and agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.formation: Masculine singular: ce before consonant, cet before vowel or mute h; feminine singular: cette; plural (masculine and feminine): ces.
usage: Pointing out specific people or things
exceptions: ce becomes cet before masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h (e.g., cet appartement, cet arbre).
agreement_rules: Agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
common_traps: Confusing ce and cet; forgetting that cet is used before vowel or mute h.

attestations.source_text: Masculine singular ce livre, cet auteur, cet homme; note that ce adds -t before masculine singular noun starting with vowel or mute h.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Using -ci and -là to distinguish between two elements
grammar_rules.summary: To distinguish between two elements, add -ci (this/these) or -là (that/those) to the noun after the demonstrative adjective.
grammar_rules.explanation: The particles -ci and -là are added to the noun following the demonstrative adjective to indicate proximity (ci) or distance (là).
usage: Making a distinction between two elements
conditions: Typically used when comparing two items or indicating a choice.
common_traps: Misplacing the particle: it is attached to the noun, not the adjective.

attestations.source_text: To make a distinction between two elements, -ci and -là are added to the noun following the demonstrative adjective.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they modify
grammar_rules.summary: Possessive adjectives express relationship/ownership and agree in gender and number with the noun, not the possessor.
grammar_rules.explanation: Possessive adjectives modify nouns and agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.formation: Masculine singular: mon, ton, son, notre, votre, leur; feminine singular: ma, ta, sa, notre, votre, leur; plural: mes, tes, ses, nos, vos, leurs.
exceptions: Mon, ton, son are used before singular feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or mute h (e.g., mon amie, ton amitié, son honnêteté).
agreement_rules: Agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
common_traps: Son, sa, ses can mean his or her; context usually disambiguates.

attestations.source_text: Possessive adjectives modify nouns and are used to express relationship and ownership. They agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Expressing possession with être à + disjunctive pronoun/noun
grammar_rules.summary: Use être à + disjunctive pronoun or noun to express possession.
grammar_rules.explanation: Another way of expressing possession is to use être à + a noun or a disjunctive pronoun.
grammar_rules.formation: être + à + disjunctive pronoun (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles) or noun
restrictions: Most common way of expressing possession.
common_traps: Using possessive adjectives instead of à + pronoun when asking whose something is.

attestations.source_text: Another way of expressing possession is to use être à + a noun or a disjunctive pronoun.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Possessive pronouns replace noun + possessive adjective
grammar_rules.summary: Possessive pronouns replace nouns used with possessive adjectives and agree with the noun replaced.
grammar_rules.explanation: Possessive pronouns (le mien, la mienne, etc.) replace a noun modified by a possessive adjective.
grammar_rules.formation: le mien / la mienne / les miens / les miennes / le tien / la tienne / les tiens / les tiennes / le sien / la sienne / les siens / les siennes / le nôtre / la nôtre / les nôtres / le vôtre / la vôtre / les vôtres / le leur / la leur / les leurs.
usage: Replacing a noun to avoid repetition
conditions: Preceded by definite article (le, la, les).
exceptions: When preceded by à or de, contractions occur: au mien, du mien, etc.
agreement_rules: Agree in gender and number with the noun replaced, not with the possessor.
common_traps: Forgetting to contract à/de with the article (au lieu de "à le mien", use "au mien").

attestations.source_text: Possessive pronouns replace nouns used with possessive adjectives. They agree in gender and number with the noun they replace, not with the possessor.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Possessive pronouns with aussi and non plus
grammar_rules.summary: Use possessive pronouns with aussi (affirmative) and non plus (negative) to confirm statements.
grammar_rules.explanation: The possessive pronoun is used with aussi to confirm an affirmative statement and with non plus to confirm a negative statement.
grammar_rules.formation: le mien aussi / le mien non plus
agreement_rules: Possessive pronoun agrees with the noun it replaces.
common_traps: Using aussi in negative contexts or non plus in affirmative contexts.

attestations.section_title: Possessive pronouns with aussi and non plus
attestations.source_text: The possessive pronoun is also often used with aussi and non plus to confirm an affirmative or negative statement.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Demonstrative pronouns replace demonstrative adjective + noun
grammar_rules.summary: Demonstrative pronouns (celui, celle, ceux, celles) replace a noun with a demonstrative adjective.
grammar_rules.explanation: A demonstrative pronoun replaces a demonstrative adjective + a noun. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it replaces.
grammar_rules.formation: Masculine singular: celui; feminine singular: celle; plural: ceux (masc./mixed), celles (fem.).
restrictions: Can be followed by -ci/-là, de, qui, que, or prepositional phrase.
agreement_rules: Agree in gender and number with noun replaced.
grammar_rules.word_order: Varies; can be subject or object.
common_traps: Forgetting to use the correct gender/number form.

attestations.source_text: A demonstrative pronoun replaces a demonstrative adjective + a noun. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it replaces.

grammar_rules.summary: Add -ci or -là to demonstrative pronouns to indicate this one or that one.
grammar_rules.explanation: Compound demonstrative pronouns are formed by adding -ci (this) or -là (that) to the demonstrative pronoun, used to compare or indicate choice.
grammar_rules.formation: celui-ci / celui-là, celle-ci / celle-là, ceux-ci / ceux-là, celles-ci / celles-là.
usage: Indicating a choice between two objects/people
restrictions: May carry derogatory meaning when referring to a person not present.
common_traps: Using with a person not present may sound condescending.

attestations.source_text: Compound demonstrative pronouns are used to compare elements of the same nature or to indicate a choice between two objects or two people.

grammar_rules.summary: Ce (c') is invariable, often subject of être, and the following adjective is always masculine singular.
grammar_rules.explanation: The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and often subject of être. It refers to an idea previously introduced. The adjective following ce is always masculine singular, even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.
usage: Referring to a previously introduced idea
restrictions: Adjective after ce is masculine singular.
agreement_rules: Adjective remains masculine singular regardless of antecedent gender.
common_traps: Making the adjective agree with the antecedent gender/number.

attestations.source_text: The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and is often the subject of the verb être. It refers to an idea previously introduced. The adjective following ce (c') is always in the masculine even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Indefinite demonstrative pronouns ceci, cela, ça
grammar_rules.summary: Ceci, cela, and ça refer to indefinite things or ideas; ceci announces, cela reflects, ça is familiar.
grammar_rules.explanation: Ceci (this) initiates a statement; cela (that) reflects on something already mentioned; ça is familiar and replaces both.
usage: Referring to indefinite things or ideas
Ceci: to announce a following sentence
Cela: to refer back to something already mentioned
common_traps: Using ceci when referring back to something already mentioned (should use cela/ça).

attestations.source_text: The indefinite demonstrative pronouns ceci (this), cela (that), and ça (this/that, familiar) refer to indefinite things or ideas. Ceci may initiate a statement and also announce a following sentence. Cela may reflect on something already mentioned.

exceptions_and_traps.title: ce vs cet before vowel or mute h
exceptions_and_traps.description: The demonstrative adjective ce adds a -t before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel or a mute h, becoming cet.

attestations.source_text: Note that the demonstrative adjective ce adds a -t before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel or a mute h (cet appartement, cet arbre).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Mon, ton, son used before feminine nouns starting with vowel/mute h
exceptions_and_traps.description: The masculine singular possessive adjectives mon, ton, son are used before singular feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or a mute h instead of ma, ta, sa.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: mon amie, ton amitié, son honnêteté
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: ma amie, ta amitié, sa honnêteté

attestations.source_text: Note that the masculine singular form of the possessive adjective (mon, ton, son) is used before singular feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or a mute h.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Ambiguity of son, sa, ses
exceptions_and_traps.description: Son, sa, ses can mean either his or her. Context usually prevents ambiguity; if ambiguity exists, the sentence should be rephrased.

attestations.source_text: Son, sa, ses can mean either his or hers, since they modify the noun (not the owner). The context will usually prevent any ambiguity about the identity of the owner. If there is ambiguity, the sentence needs to be rephrased for clarity.

exceptions_and_traps.title: être à vs possessive pronoun for possession
exceptions_and_traps.description: The most common way of expressing possession is être à + disjunctive pronoun. Possessive pronouns are used to stress ownership or identify different items of similar nature.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Cette valise est à moi. (common) / C'est le mien. (stress)

attestations.source_text: Remember that the most common way of expressing possession is by using être à + the disjunctive pronoun. When one wants to stress the ownership or identify different items of a similar nature, the possessive pronoun is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Possessive adjective vs pronoun in 'un de' constructions
exceptions_and_traps.description: Contrary to English, sometimes a possessive adjective rather than a possessive pronoun is required in French, e.g., C'est un de mes collègues (not *un de les miens).

attestations.source_text: Contrary to English, sometimes a possessive adjective rather than a possessive pronoun is required in French. C'est un de vos associés? C'est un de mes collègues.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Compound demonstrative pronouns may be derogatory
exceptions_and_traps.description: Celui-ci/celui-là (and feminine/plural forms) may carry a condescending or derogatory meaning when used to talk about a person who is not present.

attestations.source_text: Note that celui-ci (celle-ci) and celui-là (celle-là) may carry a condescending or derogatory meaning when used to talk about a person who is not present. Therefore, be careful if you decide to use it to refer to a person.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Adjective after ce (c') is always masculine singular
exceptions_and_traps.description: The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and the adjective following ce is always masculine singular, even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.

attestations.source_text: The adjective following ce (c') is always in the masculine even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.
